opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's an interesting question, and I think people often conflate two different things. One is whether the field is running out of ideas, and the other is whether each individual idea gives you as much as it used to.

From where I sit, I don't think we're running out of ideas at all. If anything, there are more people working on this than ever, and the surface area keeps growing: architectures, data, objectives, post-training, inference-time compute, evaluation. What has changed is that a lot of the "easy" wins, the things where you change one line and get a big jump, have mostly been picked. So it can feel like diminishing returns, because a single paper rarely moves the needle the way something like the original transformer or scaling laws did.

But I think that's a bit of a misleading picture. Progress now comes from stacking many smaller improvements, and their combined effect is still very large. You get a little from better data mixtures, a little from a training-stability trick, a little from a better objective, and then you scale it up and it compounds. Individually, each one looks incremental. Together, the model is clearly a generation ahead.

The other thing I'd say is that a lot of ideas don't really work until the conditions are right. Something that looked like a dead end at small scale or with weaker base models suddenly becomes very relevant once the models are strong enough. So "diminishing returns" is often a statement about the current regime rather than about the idea itself.

So my honest view is that the rate of genuinely new ideas is fine. The bar for what counts as a meaningful improvement has just gotten much higher, and the work has shifted toward careful engineering, good taste about what to try, and knowing how ideas interact at scale. That's less glamorous, but I don't think it means we're hitting a wall.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what you count as an idea. If you look at the raw number of papers, it's obviously exploded, but I don't think that tracks the number of ideas that actually move the needle. A lot of it is variations on a theme, or things that look novel at small scale and then just wash out when you train something bigger.

That's actually been one of the recurring lessons for me. When I was at Google Brain, we'd see a lot of architectural tweaks that gave you a nice bump at some modest size, and then you'd scale up and the gap would close or even reverse. The transformer is kind of remarkable in that sense, because most attempts to beat it have not really survived scale. So in that narrow sense, yes, there are diminishing returns on the "new architecture" axis. The bar for something to displace the default has gotten very high.

But I don't think the field as a whole is in diminishing returns. The frontier has shifted. The interesting ideas now are less about "what's the block" and more about data, how you mix it, how you do post-training, what you do at inference time, how you evaluate. A lot of the returns are coming from stuff that doesn't look like a clean research contribution in the classic sense. It's more like craft, and the craft compounds.

There's also a fairness thing in how we talk about this. People sometimes say "nothing new has happened since attention," and I think that's a bit unfair. Scaling itself was a bet that a lot of people didn't believe in. Instruction tuning, RLHF, mixture of experts actually working in production, long context, test-time compute. Each of those was a real idea, it just didn't arrive as a single paper with a single name attached.

So if I had to summarize: returns on any single axis diminish, that's just how it works. But the number of axes keeps growing, and I think people underestimate how much room there still is on the ones that are less glamorous. I'd be more worried about the field converging on the same recipe than about running out of ideas.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two things here. You can have diminishing returns from a particular approach, but that doesn’t necessarily mean you’re running out of new ideas. It might just mean that the recipe you’re using is getting saturated.

The hard part is that you can’t really predict when the next useful idea will arrive. Research isn’t a smooth curve where every month you get the same amount of progress. You might spend a long time making incremental improvements, and then one change opens up a whole new direction.

So I’d be careful about extrapolating from diminishing returns in one direction to diminishing returns for the entire field. At the same time, having more papers or more ideas doesn’t automatically mean more meaningful progress. The question is whether those ideas actually change what we can do.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to separate diminishing returns from a particular idea from diminishing returns in research overall. You can push one recipe for a long time, and eventually each improvement becomes more expensive. But that doesn’t mean we’ve exhausted the space of ideas. It might just mean we need a different recipe.

The tricky part is that the rate of papers isn’t necessarily the rate of new ideas. A lot of work explores variations of things that already work, which is useful, but a genuinely new direction can take longer to recognize. So I’m optimistic about research, but I wouldn’t expect progress to be smooth. You get a period of squeezing improvements out of an approach, then something changes and opens up another set of possibilities.
